items.title: List, Set, Map
items.context: List: an ordered collection that allows duplicates, accessed by index (ArrayList, LinkedList). Set: an unordered collection with no duplicates (HashSet, TreeSet). Map: key-value pairs with unique keys (HashMap, TreeMap).

questions.prompt: Which collection type allows duplicate elements and preserves insertion order via an index?
questions.explanation: List (e.g. ArrayList, LinkedList) is an ordered collection that allows duplicates and supports index-based access.

questions.prompt: Which collection interface guarantees unique keys but allows duplicate values?
questions.explanation: A Map stores key-value pairs where each key is unique, but multiple keys can map to equal values.

items.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList vs Vector
items.context: ArrayList is a dynamic array — O(1) get, O(n) insert/remove in the middle. LinkedList is a doubly linked list — O(1) insert/remove at known positions, O(n) get by index. Vector is like ArrayList but synchronized, and largely legacy.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of get(i) on an ArrayList versus a LinkedList?
choices: O(1) for ArrayList, O(n) for LinkedList
O(n) for ArrayList, O(1) for LinkedList
questions.explanation: ArrayList backs onto a real array so indexing is O(1); LinkedList must walk node-by-node from an end, making get(i) O(n).

questions.prompt: Which of these three is synchronized (thread-safe) by default?
questions.explanation: Vector's methods are synchronized, which is also why it's slower and considered legacy — prefer ArrayList plus explicit synchronization or a concurrent collection instead.

items.title: How HashMap works internally
items.context: HashMap hashes each key to compute a bucket index. Collisions in the same bucket are handled with a linked list (or a balanced tree once a bucket gets long enough in modern Java). HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values; Hashtable is synchronized and allows neither.

questions.prompt: Two different keys hash to the same bucket in a HashMap. What happens?
choices: Both entries are kept in that bucket, chained in a list (or tree)
The map automatically resizes to avoid any collision
questions.explanation: Collisions are normal and expected; HashMap keeps a chain (linked list, or a red-black tree if the chain grows long) of entries in the same bucket and compares keys with equals() when looking one up.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes HashMap from Hashtable?
choices: HashMap allows a null key, Hashtable does not
HashMap is synchronized, Hashtable is not
questions.explanation: HashMap permits one null key and multiple null values and is not synchronized; Hashtable is an older, synchronized class that rejects null keys and values entirely.

items.title: Comparable vs Comparator
items.context: Comparable defines a class's single natural ordering via compareTo(). Comparator defines an external, custom ordering via compare(), useful when you need multiple orderings or can't modify the class.

questions.prompt: Which interface requires you to modify the class itself to define its ordering?
questions.explanation: A class implements Comparable directly and provides compareTo() — that's its one 'natural' ordering.

questions.prompt: You need to sort a third-party class two different ways (by name, then separately by date) without modifying it. What do you use?
questions.explanation: Comparator lives outside the class, so you can write as many independent orderings as you need without touching the original class.

items.title: Iterator, ListIterator & Generics
items.context: Iterator traverses any collection forward only (next, hasNext, remove). ListIterator works only on Lists but also supports backward traversal, add(), and set(). Generics give compile-time type safety for collections, avoiding ClassCastException at runtime.

questions.prompt: Which of these supports traversing a list backward?
questions.explanation: ListIterator adds previous()/hasPrevious() on top of what Iterator offers, but it only works on List implementations.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit of using generics with collections?
choices: Compile-time type safety, avoiding ClassCastException at runtime
questions.explanation: Generics let the compiler catch type mismatches when you add or retrieve elements, instead of failing with a ClassCastException later at runtime.

items.title: Queues & Deques
items.context: Deque (double-ended queue) supports insertion/removal at both ends — ArrayDeque is the modern, preferred choice for stack or queue behavior over the legacy Stack class. PriorityQueue orders its elements by natural ordering or a supplied Comparator, not insertion order.

questions.prompt: Which interface represents a collection that supports adding and removing elements from both ends?
questions.explanation: Deque (double-ended queue) exposes methods like addFirst/addLast and removeFirst/removeLast for working from either end.

questions.prompt: What determines the iteration/removal order of a PriorityQueue?
choices: Natural ordering or a supplied Comparator
questions.explanation: PriorityQueue is a heap that always surfaces the smallest (or highest-priority, per its Comparator) element first, regardless of insertion order.

questions.prompt: You need LIFO stack behavior in modern Java code. What's generally preferred over java.util.Stack?
questions.explanation: java.util.Stack is a legacy class built on the synchronized Vector; ArrayDeque is faster, unsynchronized, and provides the same push()/pop() stack operations.

items.title: TreeMap & TreeSet
items.context: TreeMap and TreeSet keep their elements sorted (by natural ordering or a supplied Comparator), backed by a red-black tree — giving O(log n) get/put/contains instead of HashMap/HashSet's average O(1).

questions.prompt: What ordering guarantee does a TreeSet provide that a HashSet does not?
choices: Elements are kept in sorted order
Elements are kept in reverse insertion order
questions.explanation: TreeSet maintains its elements in sorted order (natural or via a Comparator) at all times, unlike HashSet which gives no ordering guarantee.

questions.prompt: What is the typical time complexity of get()/put() on a TreeMap?
questions.explanation: TreeMap is backed by a red-black tree, giving O(log n) for get/put/remove — slower than HashMap's average O(1), in exchange for sorted iteration order.

items.title: equals() and hashCode() contract
items.context: If two objects are equal per equals(), they must return the same hashCode() — this contract is essential for HashMap/HashSet to work correctly, since they use hashCode() to locate a bucket and equals() to confirm a match within it.

questions.prompt: If a.equals(b) returns true, what must also be true?
choices: a and b must have different hashCode() values
a and b must be the same object reference
questions.explanation: The equals/hashCode contract requires that equal objects produce equal hash codes — otherwise a HashMap/HashSet may store or 'lose' entries in the wrong bucket.

questions.prompt: You override equals() on a class but leave the default (identity-based) hashCode(). What breaks?
choices: equals() stops being called at all
Two 'equal' instances can end up in different HashMap buckets, so lookups can fail to find an entry that's logically present
The class will no longer compile
questions.explanation: Without a matching hashCode() override, two objects that are equal() can still hash to different buckets, so HashMap/HashSet lookups (which check the bucket by hash first) can silently miss a match.

items.title: Immutable & unmodifiable collections
items.context: List.of(), Set.of(), and Map.of() (Java 9+) create genuinely immutable collections. Collections.unmodifiableList() instead wraps an existing mutable list in a read-only view — the underlying list can still change if someone else holds a reference to it.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call .add() on a list created with List.of(...)?
choices: It appends normally, like any other List
questions.explanation: List.of() (and Set.of()/Map.of()) return truly immutable collections; any mutating call throws UnsupportedOperationException.

items.title: ConcurrentHashMap
items.context: ConcurrentHashMap allows safe concurrent access without locking the entire map (unlike a synchronized HashMap or the legacy Hashtable), giving much better throughput for concurrent reads and writes. Unlike HashMap, it does not permit null keys or null values.

questions.prompt: Why is ConcurrentHashMap generally preferred over wrapping a HashMap with Collections.synchronizedMap() under high concurrency?
choices: It's the only thread-safe Map implementation
It allows concurrent access without locking the whole map on every operation, giving much better throughput
questions.explanation: Collections.synchronizedMap() locks the entire map for every operation; ConcurrentHashMap uses finer-grained internal locking/lock-free techniques, so many threads can operate on it concurrently with far less contention.

questions.prompt: Does ConcurrentHashMap allow null keys or null values?
choices: No, unlike HashMap it permits neither
questions.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap disallows both null keys and null values — partly because null would make it impossible to distinguish 'no mapping' from 'mapped to null' under concurrent access.

items.title: Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators
items.context: Iterators on collections like ArrayList/HashMap are fail-fast: they detect structural modification during iteration and throw ConcurrentModificationException. Iterators on collections like CopyOnWriteArrayList or ConcurrentHashMap are fail-safe: they iterate over a stable view and don't throw, even if the collection changes underneath them.

questions.prompt: What does a fail-fast iterator do when the underlying collection is structurally modified during iteration?
questions.explanation: Fail-fast iterators (ArrayList, HashMap, ...) track a modification count and throw ConcurrentModificationException as soon as they detect it changed unexpectedly, rather than risk undefined behavior.

questions.prompt: Which kind of collection typically provides a fail-safe iterator that won't throw if the collection changes during iteration?
questions.explanation: CopyOnWriteArrayList's iterator works over a snapshot taken when iteration started, so later modifications to the live list don't affect it and never trigger ConcurrentModificationException.

items.title: HashMap resizing & load factor
items.context: HashMap starts with a default capacity and load factor (0.75). Once the number of entries exceeds capacity × load factor, it resizes (typically doubling capacity) and rehashes all entries into the new buckets — an operation that's relatively expensive if it happens often.

questions.prompt: What triggers a HashMap to resize and rehash its entries?
choices: The number of entries exceeding capacity multiplied by the load factor
Never — HashMap has a fixed size once created
questions.explanation: Once size crosses the threshold (capacity × load factor), HashMap allocates a larger bucket array and rehashes every existing entry into it.

questions.prompt: What is HashMap's default load factor?
questions.explanation: 0.75 is HashMap's default load factor — a balance Java's designers chose between memory usage (lower factor, more wasted space) and lookup performance (higher factor, more collisions).

items.title: LinkedHashMap
items.context: LinkedHashMap preserves iteration order — by default, insertion order — by maintaining a doubly-linked list through its entries alongside the normal hash table. With accessOrder=true, it can instead order entries from least- to most-recently accessed, which is the basis for a simple LRU cache via removeEldestEntry().

questions.prompt: What iteration order does a LinkedHashMap preserve by default?
choices: Random order, reshuffled on each access
questions.explanation: Unlike HashMap, LinkedHashMap threads a linked list through its entries so iteration reflects insertion order by default (or access order, if configured).

questions.prompt: You want a simple bounded LRU cache with minimal code. Which built-in class gets you most of the way there?
choices: LinkedHashMap configured with accessOrder=true, overriding removeEldestEntry()
questions.explanation: LinkedHashMap with accessOrder=true reorders entries by recency of access, and overriding removeEldestEntry() to return true past a size threshold turns it into a working LRU cache with very little code.

items.title: Collections.sort() and natural ordering
items.context: Collections.sort(list) with no explicit Comparator requires the elements to implement Comparable — calling it on a list of a class that doesn't provide a natural ordering fails at runtime, not compile time.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call Collections.sort(list) with no Comparator, on a list of objects whose class does not implement Comparable?
choices: It compiles and sorts by object identity
It silently leaves the list unsorted
questions.explanation: Collections.sort(List<T>) with no Comparator requires T to implement Comparable; without it, the sort's internal comparisons fail at runtime with a ClassCastException, since the generic signature can't catch this at compile time for an arbitrary class.

items.title: Arrays.asList() pitfalls
items.context: Arrays.asList(array) returns a fixed-size list backed directly by the array — you can set() elements, but add()/remove() throw UnsupportedOperationException because the list can't change size.

questions.prompt: What happens if you call .add() on a list returned by Arrays.asList(...)?
choices: It replaces the entire underlying array
It throws UnsupportedOperationException, since the list is fixed-size
It appends normally like any ArrayList
questions.explanation: Arrays.asList() wraps the array directly rather than copying it, so it supports set() but not structural changes like add()/remove() — those throw UnsupportedOperationException.

items.title: Bulk collection operations
items.context: retainAll() keeps only the elements also present in another collection (set intersection). removeAll() removes every element that appears in another collection (set difference).

questions.prompt: What does listA.retainAll(listB) do to listA?
choices: Keeps only the elements of listA that are also present in listB, removing the rest
Sorts listA using listB as a reference order
Removes every element of listA that's in listB
Adds every element of listB into listA
questions.explanation: retainAll() mutates the collection to keep only elements found in the argument collection — effectively a set intersection performed in place.

items.title: EnumMap & EnumSet
items.context: EnumMap and EnumSet are specialized, highly efficient Map/Set implementations for keys that are enum constants — internally backed by an array indexed by the enum's ordinal, faster and more compact than a general-purpose HashMap/HashSet of enums.

questions.prompt: Why prefer EnumMap over a HashMap<SomeEnum, V> when the keys are all enum constants?
choices: EnumMap is backed by a compact array indexed by ordinal, making it faster and more memory-efficient for enum keys
EnumMap supports keys of any type, not just enums
EnumMap allows null keys, HashMap doesn't
questions.explanation: Because an enum's set of possible values is fixed and known, EnumMap can use a simple array indexed by ordinal() instead of general hashing — smaller and faster than HashMap for this specific case.

items.title: ArrayList's default capacity
items.context: An ArrayList created with the no-argument constructor starts with a default internal array capacity of 10, growing (typically by 50%) once that capacity is exceeded.

questions.prompt: What is the default initial capacity of an ArrayList created with `new ArrayList<>()`?
questions.explanation: ArrayList's no-arg constructor starts with a backing array capacity of 10; it grows automatically (roughly by 50%) once more elements are added than it can currently hold.

items.title: Why String is a popular HashMap key
items.context: String is immutable, caches its hashCode() after first computing it, and has a well-defined equals() based on content — all three properties make it fast and safe to use as a HashMap key, since its hash can never change after insertion.

questions.prompt: Why is String such a common choice for HashMap keys?
choices: String is immutable with a cached hashCode() and well-defined equals(), so its hash can never change after being used as a key
Strings automatically sort themselves in a HashMap
Strings are always short, so hashing is fast
questions.explanation: A HashMap key's hashCode() must stay consistent for the lifetime of its entry — immutability guarantees that, String caches its hash so repeated lookups are cheap, and equals() reliably compares by content rather than reference.

items.title: The fail-fast modCount mechanism
items.context: Fail-fast collections track a modCount field, incremented on every structural change. Each iterator snapshots modCount when created and compares it on every next() call — a mismatch means the collection changed outside the iterator, triggering ConcurrentModificationException.

questions.prompt: How does a fail-fast iterator actually detect that its collection was structurally modified?
choices: It re-scans the entire collection before every element
It compares a modification counter (modCount) snapshotted at iterator creation against the collection's current modCount on each step
It uses a lock that blocks all other modification
It relies on the garbage collector to notify it
questions.explanation: ArrayList/HashMap (and friends) keep an internal modCount incremented on structural changes; each iterator remembers the modCount it saw at creation and checks for a mismatch on every next(), throwing ConcurrentModificationException the moment it detects one.

items.title: subList() is a live view
items.context: List.subList(from, to) doesn't copy anything — it returns a view backed by the original list. Structural changes made through either the sublist or the original list are reflected in both, and can invalidate the sublist view (throwing ConcurrentModificationException on next access) if the original list is modified directly.

questions.prompt: You take list.subList(0, 3) and then call list.add(...) directly on the original list. What happens if you then use the sublist?
choices: The sublist may throw ConcurrentModificationException, since it's a live view invalidated by structural changes to the backing list
The sublist automatically resizes to include the new element
The sublist silently ignores the change
questions.explanation: subList() returns a view, not a copy — structurally modifying the backing list through any other reference invalidates that view, and subsequent use of the sublist throws ConcurrentModificationException.

items.title: Capacity vs size
items.context: An ArrayList's size() is the number of elements actually stored; its internal capacity (the backing array's length) is normally larger, to leave room for growth without resizing on every single add().

questions.prompt: For an ArrayList, what is the relationship between its capacity and its size()?
choices: Capacity is always smaller than size()
Capacity and size are unrelated concepts
Capacity is the backing array's length and is generally >= size(), leaving room to grow without resizing on every add()
questions.explanation: size() reports how many elements are actually present; capacity is how many the current backing array could hold before a resize is needed — keeping capacity ahead of size avoids reallocating on every single insertion.

items.title: Collections.synchronizedList vs concurrent collections
items.context: Collections.synchronizedList(list) wraps a list so each individual method call is synchronized on one shared lock — but iterating it still requires manual synchronization to avoid ConcurrentModificationException. Purpose-built concurrent collections (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap) are designed for safe concurrent iteration without that extra step.

questions.prompt: If you iterate a list wrapped with Collections.synchronizedList() without any extra precautions, what can happen?
choices: Another thread modifying the list concurrently can still cause a ConcurrentModificationException during iteration, since only individual calls are synchronized, not the whole iteration
It silently returns an empty list
Nothing — synchronizedList makes iteration completely safe automatically
questions.explanation: synchronizedList() only synchronizes each individual method call; iterating still requires the caller to manually synchronize on the list for the duration of the loop, unlike purpose-built concurrent collections designed for safe concurrent iteration.

items.title: HashSet is backed by HashMap
items.context: Internally, HashSet is implemented as a thin wrapper around a HashMap instance — each element is stored as a key in that map, mapped to a single shared dummy constant value, since only the keys (uniqueness) actually matter for a Set.

questions.prompt: What data structure does HashSet use internally to store its elements?
choices: A HashMap, where each element is stored as a key mapped to a constant dummy value
Its own custom hash table unrelated to HashMap
questions.explanation: HashSet delegates to an internal HashMap<E, Object>, storing each set element as a key against a single shared placeholder value — HashSet's uniqueness and performance characteristics come directly from HashMap's.

items.title: Null handling differs across Map implementations
items.context: HashMap and LinkedHashMap allow one null key and multiple null values. TreeMap throws a NullPointerException on a null key (with the natural ordering comparator), since it needs to compare keys to place them in sorted order, and null can't be compared.

questions.prompt: What happens if you try to put a null key into a TreeMap using natural ordering?
choices: It's accepted just like in HashMap
TreeMap converts null to an empty string
It throws NullPointerException, since TreeMap needs to compare keys to sort them and null can't be compared
It silently replaces the first entry
questions.explanation: TreeMap maintains sorted order via comparisons; since null has no defined ordering relative to other keys, attempting to insert a null key with the default natural-ordering comparator throws NullPointerException — unlike HashMap, which happily allows one null key.

items.title: Sizing collections upfront
items.context: Specifying an initial capacity (new ArrayList<>(1000), new HashMap<>(1000)) when you already know roughly how many elements you'll add avoids repeated internal resizing/rehashing as the collection grows past its default small capacity.

questions.prompt: Why might you pass an initial capacity to an ArrayList or HashMap constructor instead of using the default?
choices: It avoids the overhead of repeated resizing/rehashing as the collection grows toward a known target size
questions.explanation: Growing a collection typically means allocating a bigger backing array/table and copying everything over; if you already know approximately how many elements are coming, sizing it upfront avoids several of those reallocation-and-copy steps.

items.title: Set.of() rejects duplicates outright
items.context: Unlike building a HashSet from a list that happens to contain duplicates (which just silently keeps one copy), calling Set.of(a, b, a) with a literal duplicate throws IllegalArgumentException immediately, since an immutable factory method treats that as a caller error.

questions.prompt: What happens when you call Set.of("a", "b", "a") with a repeated argument?
choices: It throws IllegalArgumentException at creation time
It creates a List instead of a Set
It silently creates a set with one "a"
questions.explanation: Set.of(...) treats a literal duplicate argument as a programming mistake and throws IllegalArgumentException immediately — different from constructing a HashSet from a collection that happens to contain duplicates, which just quietly deduplicates.

items.title: Modifying a list during for-each

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
choices: Prints "[Ann, Bo, Cy]" — the remove is ignored
questions.explanation: Removing from a List while iterating it with a for-each loop (which uses the List's own Iterator) invalidates the iterator's internal modCount check — the next call to next() or hasNext() throws ConcurrentModificationException.

items.title: Iterator.remove() vs list.remove()

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Iterator.remove() is the safe way to remove during iteration — it updates the iterator's own bookkeeping, so no ConcurrentModificationException is thrown. Compare this with removing directly from the list in a for-each loop.

items.title: Integer cache and ==

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: Integer.valueOf() caches boxed values from -128 to 127. Both a and b are autoboxed 100s, so they point to the same cached object (true). 200 is outside the cache range, so x and y are distinct objects (false). Always use .equals() to compare wrapper values.

items.title: new Integer() bypasses the cache

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: new Integer(...) always allocates a fresh object, bypassing the Integer cache entirely — even for a value inside the cached range. Integer.valueOf(127) returns the cached instance, so a and b are different objects and == is false. (new Integer(int) is deprecated since Java 9 for exactly this kind of confusion.)

items.title: List.of() is immutable

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: List.of(...) returns an immutable list. Any structural mutation — add, remove, set — throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime; it's not caught at compile time because add() is still a valid List method.

items.title: Unboxing a null Integer

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: 10 + count requires unboxing count to an int so the + operator can work. Unboxing null calls count.intValue() on a null reference, throwing NullPointerException — a classic autoboxing trap in arithmetic and ternary expressions.

items.title: Mutating a HashMap key after insertion

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: HashMap buckets a key by its hashCode() at insertion time. Mutating k.id after insertion changes its hashCode, so a later get(k) looks in the wrong bucket and finds nothing (null). A fresh Key(2) hashes to that same wrong bucket too and also finds nothing — the entry is effectively lost. Never mutate fields that a HashMap key's equals()/hashCode() depend on.

items.title: TreeSet with a comparator that ties

questions.prompt: What does this print?
questions.explanation: A TreeSet orders and de-duplicates using its Comparator, not equals(). "cat" and "dog" both have length 3, so the comparator returns 0 for that pair and the set treats "dog" as a duplicate — it's silently not added. Only "cat" (length 3, first in) and "bear" (length 4) remain, so size() is 2.

items.title: PECS: writing to a ? extends list
items.context:
List<? extends Number> nums = new ArrayList<Integer>();
nums.add(42);

questions.prompt: What happens when this code is compiled?
choices: Compile error on the add() call
questions.explanation: A `? extends Number` wildcard means "some unknown subtype of Number" — the compiler can't guarantee it's specifically an Integer, so it refuses any add() except null. This is the "Producer Extends, Consumer Super" (PECS) rule: extends wildcards are read-only for writes.

items.title: Generic type erasure and unchecked raw types

questions.prompt: What happens when this code runs?
questions.explanation: Generics are erased at compile time, so the raw-typed reference lets `set(42)` compile with only an unchecked warning — an Integer is stored where a String is expected. The ClassCastException doesn't happen at that assignment; it happens later at box.get().length(), when the compiler-inserted cast to String finally runs against the actual Integer, since Java enforces generics via casts injected at the read site.
